knowledgePattern: Connect the sums of original, squared and alternating geometric sequences

hints.title: Write the three progressions
hints.body: Name the original first term and ratio. Then write a few terms of the squared and alternating sequences to identify their first terms and ratios.
hints.recap: Powers and alternating signs modify a GP’s first term and common ratio in different ways.
hints.pitfall: Squaring a sum is not the same as summing squared terms.
hints.pause: Express the known sums and the requested sum using the GP formula.

recall.reminder: Powers and alternating signs modify a GP’s first term and common ratio in different ways.

hints.title: Factor the denominators
hints.body: Look for a difference of squares in the known formulas. It may connect their sums without solving for each parameter.
hints.recap: Factoring can reveal common parts before elimination or cancellation.
hints.pitfall: Check convergence for the alternating progression as well.
hints.pause: Relate the formulas and evaluate the unknown sum.

recall.reminder: Factoring can reveal common parts before elimination or cancellation.

solution:
1. Let un=arn−1. A finite nonzero sum to infinity implies |r|<1, and a/(1−r)=3. Squaring every term gives a2/(1−r2)=6.

2. The alternating sequence starts a,−ar,ar2,−ar3,…, so its ratio is −r and its sum is V=a/(1+r). It also converges because |−r|<1.

3. Using 1−r2=(1−r)(1+r) gives 6=a1−ra1+r=3V. Therefore V=2. Answer C.
